title: Terraform state consistency seatbelt probes for private deployments
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight troubleshooting playbook focused on Terraform state consistency, drift detection, and low-risk seatbelt probes to run before, during, and after private-deploy Terraform module upgrades (VPC and on-prem packages). It is intentionally prescriptive and short — designed for first responder engineers and solutions leads who need fast, repeatable checks to rule out common state and backend failures.

When to use:
- Before a module upgrade or patch (validate state and lock health).
- After partial apply or failed upgrade that left resources in an unknown state.
- When customers report repeated provisioning errors (timeouts, duplicate resources, provider conflicts).
- As a step in RCA for upgrade blips that resolve after state fixes.

High-level hypotheses we cover:
1) Remote state backend malfunction or lock contention (S3/Dynamo/consul/terraform cloud).
2) Drift due to out-of-band changes (manual edits in cloud/on-prem infra).
3) Provider version changes or module source updates that cause subtle schema drift.
4) Partial applies/taints left by failed upgrades (resource instances with mismatched attributes).
5) Secrets or var interpolation causing plan/apply divergence (sensitive fields masked).

Quick seatbelt checklist (5–12 minutes)
- Confirm backend health: can we read and lock state?
  - terraform init -backend-config=... && terraform state pull > /tmp/state.json (should succeed)
  - If using S3 backend: check S3 object existence + Dynamo lock TTLs in console.
- Verify workspace: terraform workspace show (ensure correct workspace/namespace)
- Basic plan sanity: terraform plan -target=module.bootstrap -refresh=true -out=/tmp/quick.plan (should run fast; failure -> backend/provider error)
- List suspicious resources: terraform state list | grep -E "aws_instance|k8s_.*|module\.private.*" | head -n 20
- Check for provider version drift: cat .terraform.lock.hcl | grep provider || (ask: who bumped the provider?)
- Confirm Git tag/module source pinned: inspect module sources in root module and compare commit/tag in module cache (if present)

Deeper probes (15–60 minutes)
1) Remote state integrity
   - Pull state and diff against last known good state (if we keep snapshots):
     - terraform state pull > /tmp/current.json
     - curl -sS "https://storage.company.internal/terraform-snapshots/<deploy>/latest.json" > /tmp/previous.json
     - jq -S . /tmp/current.json > /tmp/current.sorted && jq -S . /tmp/previous.json > /tmp/previous.sorted && diff -u /tmp/previous.sorted /tmp/current.sorted
   - Look for duplicated IDs, missing top-level modules, or unexpectedly empty resources arrays.
   - If state is corrupt (parse errors): recover from snapshot and re-lock backend before any writes.

2) Lock contention and partial apply fingerprints
   - Check locks: DynamoDB lock table entries (owner info, session id). For Consul/TF Cloud, use the UI/CLI to view locks.
   - If a stale lock exists for > 20 minutes and TLDR owner host is offline -> safely remove lock after coordination with oncall and customer. Document lock-id and reason.

3) Detect out-of-band (manual) changes
   - Run terraform plan -refresh=true and search for many resource diffs or replacements. Large numbers of diffs often imply manual edits.
   - Pull cloud provider audit logs (GCP/AWS) for recent changes to the affected resources.
   - If manual changes are intended, add import blocks or update modules to reflect intended state in a controlled rollout.

4) Provider/module schema mismatch
   - Compare provider versions between recent successful deploys and the failing run (terraform providers lock file vs last release branch).
   - For module schema differences: run terraform 0.14/1.x (matching customer) locally with module pinned to source=git::...@<commit> to reproduce plan output.

5) Taint/replace and partial resource cleanup
   - List resources with expected instances > actual instances in state -> possible partial creates.
   - Use terraform state rm to remove orphan state entries (only after verification) or terraform import to re-associate live resources.

Safe rollback/minimal-impact remediation steps
- If state is consistent but plan will replace many resources, first run targeted apply on a canary module (eg module.bootstrap or module.network) in a sandboxed workspace.
- If state is corrupt or mismatched, restore last snapshot to a staging workspace and run terraform plan to validate.
- Never directly edit state in production without peer review; prefer import/rm operations.

Commands & quick references (copyable)
- Init & pull state:
  terraform init -input=false -backend-config=\"bucket=redwood-priv-<env>\"
  terraform state pull > /tmp/state-$(date +%s).json
- Fast plan for networking module (non-destructive):
  terraform plan -refresh=true -target=module.network -out=/tmp/net.plan
- List state resources with counts:
  terraform state list | sed -E 's/(.*)\[(.*)\]/\1/g' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 40

Escalation and postmortem notes
- If probes show backend corruption or loss of state snapshots: page eng-infra and bring in the SRE oncall. Capture backend logs (S3 access logs / DynamoDB ops / consul serf logs).
- If plan differences point to provider bugs (schema changes, breaking behaviour across provider versions) -> open a minimal repro in a new GH repo, ping applied-ml or runtime team if it touches runtime modules.
- Log all state edits, imports, and lock removals in the Jira ticket. Attach state snapshots (redact secrets).

Notes to self / common gotchas seen in the field
- CI sometimes runs terraform in the wrong workspace (look for workspace==\"default\" when customer uses named).
- S3 eventual consistency can manifest as intermittent object-not-found on state pull; use retries and check Dynamo lock first.
- Secrets masked in state appear as \"<sensitive>\" and can make drift analysis noisy; export sanitized copies for diffs.
- Customers occasionally run terraform apply from a forked module with a local change; module sources must be pinned and audited.

Follow-ups and improvements (future work)
- Add an automated small-runner script to pull state, run a set of heuristics, and produce a triage summary (OK/warn/error).
- Consolidate state snapshots per-customer with TTL-based lifecycle so we can always recover last-good.
- Add a short runbook for safe state edits and a checklist to include in customer runbooks.

References and useful links:
- CONFLUENCE: Private Deploy Terraform runbooks (CONFLUENCE-PRIVDEP-782)
- GitHub PR: GITHUB-PR-1248 (module pinning changes)
- Example Jira for escalations: JIRA-OPS-5903
